paragraphs.source_en: Even so, my anxiety still would not leave me. I wondered why this should be, and after thinking it over and over, I at last understood. My vexation came from the fact that I could not arrive at a clear answer as to which of my three battle plans would be the most advantageous. If they came from the cupboard, I had a strategy to meet them. If they appeared from the bathroom, I also had a plan for dealing with them. And if they crawled up from the sink, I had a scheme ready to receive them there as well. But to decide with certainty from which of these three directions they would come gave me the greatest trouble. They say Admiral Togo was once greatly troubled because he could not tell whether the Russian Baltic Fleet would pass through the Tsushima Strait, head for the Tsugaru Strait, or take the longer way around by the Soya Strait. When I consider my own circumstances, my difficulty is one that fully deserves sympathy. Judged by my whole situation, I not only closely resembled His Excellency Togo, but in this particular problem too I shared His Excellency Togo's very anguish of deliberation.

paragraphs.source_en: While I was thus absorbed in desperately devising every possible stratagem, the torn half-height paper door suddenly opened, and the cook O-san's face thrust itself out without warning. When I say only her face appeared, I do not mean that she had no hands or feet; rather, in the dim night her other parts were hard to make out, while that vividly colored face alone first struck my eye. O-san's face was redder even than her usual red face; having apparently learned from last night's lesson, she had returned from the bathhouse and promptly barred the kitchen door. From the study came the master's shout: “Put my walking stick beside my pillow!” Why he should want a walking stick placed by his pillow was quite beyond my understanding. Surely he was not imitating Jing Ke, that brave man of the Yi River, and indulging in some fancy of clasping a sword while listening for the dragon's cry. Yesterday it was a yam by the pillow, today a walking stick; what will he put there tomorrow?

paragraphs.source_en: There is no skylight in the master's kitchen; instead, a hole about one foot wide is cut where a transom would be in a sitting room, and summer and winter alike it serves as a substitute skylight for ventilation. A gust of wind came blowing in, carrying with it the easily scattered petals of the cherry blossoms, and startled me awake. Opening my eyes, I saw that the hazy moonlight had somehow slipped indoors, and the black shadow of the stove lay slantwise across the lift-up floorboard. Fearing I might have overslept, I twitched my ears and listened for the state of the house; it was as silent as before, with only the wall clock ticking away. It was already the hour when mice appear. From where would they come?

paragraphs.source_en: From inside the cupboard came a little clattering sound, as though they were pressing a paw against the rim of a small dish while gnawing at what was inside. I thought, “What if they come out from here?” I crouched beside the broken hole and waited. It did not look as though they would come out easily. The sound of the little dish soon stopped; next they seemed to have climbed onto a large bowl or something of the kind, for from time to time there came a heavy thudding noise. They were just on the other side of the cupboard door, less than three inches from the tip of my nose. Now and then the enemy's little footsteps came pattering up to the mouth of the hole and then receded, yet not a single mouse showed its face. To have the enemy freely raging behind that one cupboard door while I could only hold my breath and wait at the exit of the hole was truly maddening. The mice were holding a dance among the dishes and bowls. If only the cook O-san had opened the cupboard door even a little, leaving just enough space for me to squeeze inside. But now the cupboard door was perversely shut tight. What a fool she is.

paragraphs.source_en: Suddenly, in the shadow of the stove, the abalone shell I used as a food dish gave a little clink. I thought, “Excellent, the enemy has appeared from this direction.” I crept softly toward it, but in the gap by the water bucket I saw only a mouse's tail flash once before it vanished under the sink. A little later, in the bathroom, the rinsing bowl struck the brass basin with a sharp clang. I thought, “Aha! Now they are attacking from the rear.” The instant I turned around, a great mouse fully half a foot long kicked down the tooth-powder bag with a slap and darted under the floorboards. I must not let it escape! I leapt down after it at once, but the fellow had already disappeared without a trace. Catching mice, it seems, is not nearly as easy as one imagines. Perhaps I was born without any talent for catching them.
